# THE SUTTON COUNTY TRANSCRIPTS

**Compiled Document, Sutton County Courthouse Archive**
**Case File: State of Missouri v. Eleanor P. Vance, No. 84-CR-00217**
**Filed: Clerk's Office, Sutton County Circuit Court**

---

## PART ONE: LET THE RECORD REFLECT

---

**OFFICIAL TRANSCRIPT — STATE OF MISSOURI v. ELEANOR P. VANCE**
**Case No. 84-CR-00217**
**Circuit Court of Sutton County, Missouri**
**The Honorable Raymond W. Kehoe, Presiding**
**Day One — Monday, September 10, 1984**
**Court Reporter: Linda A. Meszaros, CSR-MO #4407**

---

[9:02 A.M.]

THE COURT: Good morning. We are on the record in the matter of the State of Missouri versus Eleanor Patricia Vance, Case Number 84-CR-00217. Let the record reflect that the defendant is present and seated with counsel, Mr. David Fenn of the Public Defender's office. The State is represented by Assistant Prosecuting Attorney Mr. Glenn Harbaugh. We are convened for the purpose of jury selection. Before we bring in the venire panel, are there any preliminary matters?

MR. HARBAUGH: None from the State, Your Honor.

MR. FENN: Your Honor, the defense renews its motion for change of venue. Given the extent of pretrial publicity in this county—

THE COURT: That motion was denied on August twenty-third, Mr. Fenn. The ruling stands. Let's proceed.

MR. FENN: Noted for the record, Your Honor.

THE COURT: So noted. Bailiff, please bring in the panel.

[9:04 A.M. — Venire panel of forty-six (46) prospective jurors enters courtroom.]

THE COURT: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. You have been called here today as prospective jurors in a criminal matter. I want to thank you for your service. I'm going to read a brief statement, and then the attorneys will have an opportunity to ask you some questions. I ask that you listen carefully and answer honestly. There are no wrong answers. We simply need to determine whether you can be fair and impartial in this case.

THE COURT: The defendant, Eleanor Patricia Vance, age thirty-one, has been charged with three counts of murder in the first degree and three counts of abuse of a child, arising from events alleged to have occurred between January and June of 1984 at the defendant's residence at 1614 Polk Mill Road, where she served as a licensed foster parent. The alleged victims are Tamara Reese, age seven; Dylan Reese, age five; and Cody Allen Briggs, age four. The State's theory includes allegations of ritualistic conduct. I will instruct you more specifically as the trial proceeds. At this time I will ask: does any member of the panel have personal knowledge of the defendant, the alleged victims, or the facts of this case beyond what you may have read or heard in the news?

[Seven (7) prospective jurors raise hands. Individual voir dire conducted at sidebar, 9:11–9:48 A.M. See sealed sidebar transcript, Exhibit S-1.]

THE COURT: Thank you. Mr. Harbaugh, you may address the panel.

MR. HARBAUGH: Thank you, Your Honor. Good morning, folks. I'm going to ask some questions that might seem a little unusual. Bear with me. First: does anyone here have strong feelings, one way or the other, about the existence of the devil?

[Laughter from several panel members.]

PROSPECTIVE JUROR #14: Like, do I believe in the devil?

MR. HARBAUGH: That's the question, ma'am.

PROSPECTIVE JUROR #14: I'm a Baptist, so—yes.

MR. HARBAUGH: That's fine, ma'am. Anyone else? Just a show of hands. This isn't a test.

[Approximately twenty-two (22) hands raised.]

MR. HARBAUGH: All right. Now — and I want you to think carefully about this — is there anyone here who believes they would be unable to evaluate evidence of so-called "ritualistic" or "occult" practices in a rational, impartial manner? Anyone who feels that the subject matter itself would prevent them from focusing on the facts?

[No hands raised.]

MR. HARBAUGH: Thank you.

[Voir dire continues. Individual juror questioning, 9:52 A.M.–12:17 P.M. Lunch recess, 12:17–1:30 P.M. Voir dire resumes 1:30 P.M.; jury of twelve plus two alternates seated and sworn by 3:44 P.M.]

THE COURT: Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, you have been sworn. I'm going to release you for the day. We will begin with opening statements tomorrow morning at nine o'clock. A few instructions. You are not to discuss this case with anyone, including each other, until I tell you it is time to deliberate. You are not to read newspaper accounts or watch television reports about this case. You are not to visit any locations mentioned in the proceedings. If anyone attempts to contact you about this case, you are to report it to my clerk immediately. The case is in recess until nine A.M. tomorrow.

[3:47 P.M. — Court in recess.]

---

**OFFICIAL TRANSCRIPT — Day Two — Tuesday, September 11, 1984**

[9:03 A.M.]

THE COURT: Good morning. All parties are present, the jury is seated. Mr. Harbaugh, the State may proceed with its opening statement.

MR. HARBAUGH: Thank you, Your Honor.

MR. HARBAUGH: Ladies and gentlemen. Over the next several weeks, you are going to hear testimony that is unlike anything most of you have encountered. I want to prepare you for that. This is not a case about a moment of rage or a tragic accident. This is a case about sustained, deliberate, ritualized cruelty inflicted on three children who had already been failed by every adult in their lives — children who were placed in the defendant's care by the State of Missouri, which believed they would be safe.

MR. HARBAUGH: The evidence will show that between January and June of 1984, the defendant, Eleanor Vance, subjected Tamara Reese, Dylan Reese, and Cody Allen Briggs to physical and psychological abuse of an extreme nature, including confinement, starvation, burning, and the forced participation in rituals of a quasi-religious or occult character. The evidence will show that these acts were not random but followed a pattern — a calendar, if you will — tied to specific dates that hold significance in certain occult traditions. You will hear expert testimony about the nature of these traditions. You will see photographic evidence. I tell you now: some of it will be very difficult to look at.

MR. HARBAUGH: The evidence will show that all three children died as a result of injuries sustained during these acts. Tamara Reese on March fourteenth. Dylan Reese on April thirtieth. Cody Allen Briggs on June twenty-first. You will hear from the medical examiner, Dr. Reba Olson, about the cause and manner of each death. You will hear from investigators who searched the defendant's home and discovered items consistent with occult ritual practice. You will hear from the defendant's own neighbors, who will describe what they heard through the walls.

MR. HARBAUGH: And you will hear from the defendant herself. Because Eleanor Vance, through the course of these proceedings, will not be silent. I suspect she will not be able to be silent. And I ask you to listen carefully when she speaks, because the State believes that what you hear will confirm everything the evidence already shows.

MR. HARBAUGH: At the end of this trial, the State will ask you to find the defendant guilty on all counts. Thank you.

THE COURT: Thank you, Mr. Harbaugh. Mr. Fenn?

MR. FENN: Thank you, Your Honor. Ladies and gentlemen—

[Defense opening statement, 9:18 A.M.–9:47 A.M. Mr. Fenn presents alternative theory: defendant suffered untreated psychotic disorder; children's deaths resulted from neglect during defendant's decompensation, not premeditated ritual conduct. Argues for lesser included offenses. Full text follows.]

---

**AUDIO DIARY — LINDA MESZAROS**
**Monday, September 10, 1984**
**[Tape 1, Side A — 8:47 P.M.]**

[Background: Television audio, low. Occasional clink of a spoon against ceramic. Hum of a refrigerator compressor cycling on at approximately 9:02 P.M.]

Today was jury selection. Nothing unusual about it except the charge sheet, which I suppose is unusual enough. Three counts murder one, three counts child abuse. The defendant is a former foster parent. I've done worse — or I should say, I've done cases with worse courtroom atmospheres. The Blaylock trial in '79 had a packed gallery every day and someone threw a shoe at the defense table during closing arguments. This one was fairly quiet. Small gallery. Two reporters that I could count, one from the Sutton *Courier* and one I didn't recognize. The cameras the judge was worried about didn't materialize.

The courtroom is Room 4, which I don't usually draw. The fluorescent fixture directly above my station has a bad ballast. It puts out a hum at — I don't know the note, but it's steady, and it's the kind of frequency that sits right behind your eyes after an hour. I'll put in a maintenance request tomorrow if I remember. Probably I won't remember.

The defendant. I will describe her because that is what I do, I describe things, or rather I record things; describing is more than my job requires. Eleanor Vance is small. Not short, particularly, but small in the way some people are who seem to have pressed themselves inward over many years. Brown hair, flat and unwashed, cut to the jaw. She sat with her hands flat on the defense table, both palms down, all ten fingers spread. She sat like that for six hours. I watched her when I could, during sidebars, when my hands were free. She never adjusted her fingers. Even when Mr. Fenn leaned over to speak to her, she didn't move her hands. She moved her head toward him slightly, the way you'd incline your ear toward a sound you weren't sure you'd heard. Then she moved it back.

I should note for my own records — this is just housekeeping — I was not the original reporter assigned to this case. Deborah Kessler had it. Deborah took medical leave in August, and I was reassigned from the Probate division, which was fine by me. Probate is death by a thousand whereas and wherefores. I don't know what's wrong with Deborah. We aren't close. I hope she's all right.

I should also note that I am only recording these diaries because I've started doing it for all my capital cases, ever since the Blaylock appeal came back with a challenge to the transcript accuracy and I had to go through my notes line by line for three weeks. If anything gets challenged on this one, I want a contemporaneous personal record. That's all this is.

The light in Room 4 hums at — I keep coming back to it. It's not a pitch, exactly. More like a pressure. Like someone leaning on a frequency just below what the ear properly hears. I noticed the defendant tilt her head toward it once, during a sidebar. The same inclination. As if she were listening to someone speak.

Tomorrow is opening statements. I need to replace the ink ribbon on my backup machine.

[Tape 1, Side A ends — 9:14 P.M.]

---

**AUDIO DIARY — LINDA MESZAROS**
**Tuesday, September 11, 1984**
**[Tape 1, Side B — 9:31 P.M.]**

[Background: Running water in a sink, turned off at 9:32. Silence afterward, then the click of a lamp switch.]

Harbaugh's opening was competent. A little theatrical, but that's his style — he wants the jury frightened before they see the photographs, so the photographs confirm a feeling they already have rather than introducing one. It's effective. I've watched him do it before.

Fenn's opening was adequate. I don't think he believes in his own case. I think he is going through the motions of a defense because a defense is required. He argued diminished capacity without once looking at his client, which tells me everything.

Eleanor was silent today. Hands in the same position. I don't think she blinked for the first forty minutes. That isn't in the transcript, of course. No one asks the stenographer what the defendant's eyes did.

I went back and listened to my backup tape from today. I don't usually do that — the backup is for insurance, not review. But I wanted to hear Harbaugh's opening again. Something in his cadence. I couldn't identify it during the session because I was writing, and when I'm writing I process language structurally, not aurally — I hear syllables and stresses, not meaning. It's a particular mode of attention. Nonliterate people don't understand it. They think I'm a typist. I am not a typist. I am a machine that converts sound into symbols in real time, and to do that I must hear language the way a prism sees light: broken into its components.

What I heard on playback was this: at the end of Harbaugh's opening, when he said "she will not be able to be silent," the fluorescent fixture was humming, and the hum shifted. I don't mean it changed — I mean it *shifted*, the way a voice shifts register when moving from speech to recitation. A tonal adjustment. It held the new frequency for seven seconds and then returned.

I'm sure it's the ballast. I put in the maintenance request this morning. I'm sure it's the ballast.

I'm going to bed.

[Tape 1, Side B ends — 9:38 P.M.]

**OFFICIAL TRANSCRIPT — Day Three — Wednesday, September 12, 1984**

[2:14 P.M. — Prosecution witness Dr. Reba Olson, Chief Medical Examiner, Sutton County, on the stand. Direct examination by Mr. Harbaugh, regarding autopsy findings for Tamara Reese.]

MR. HARBAUGH: Dr. Olson, I'm going to direct your attention to the photographs marked State's Exhibit 14 through 14-F. Can you describe for the jury what these images show?

DR. OLSON: These are photographs of the decedent's dorsal torso — her back — taken during autopsy. Exhibits 14 and 14-A show the full dorsal view. 14-B through 14-F are close-ups of specific wound areas.

MR. HARBAUGH: Can you describe the wounds?

DR. OLSON: The decedent presented with a series of incised wounds — cuts — arranged in a pattern across the upper and middle back. There were seventeen individual incisions, varying in length from approximately two centimeters to approximately nine centimeters. They were made with a sharp, thin-bladed instrument. The cuts were not random. They were — I would characterize them as deliberate, symmetrical, and consistent with a purposeful design.

MR. HARBAUGH: When you say "design," Doctor—

THE DEFENDANT: Ahk-sah neh-ruhm voh-lahn tem seh-kuh-lee seh-kuh-loh-rum.

THE COURT: Ms. Vance—

THE DEFENDANT: Ahk-sah neh-ruhm. Ahk-sah neh-ruhm. Ahk-sah neh-ruhm.

THE COURT: Mr. Fenn, control your client.

MR. FENN: Eleanor. Eleanor, you need to stop.

THE DEFENDANT: [Continuing] Sed-dehm pah-rah-tuhm. Vas eh-lehk-tuhm.
